sentences: Late at night, at the corner of a wall, a young scholar holding a lantern faces a woman whose cloak is drawn over her head.
This is Shin Yun-bok's Lovers Under the Moon.
Let's look at it together for a moment.
The scene comes from the Hyewon album, thirty leaves of genre painting.
The collector Jeon Hyeong-pil went to Japan to bring the album home, and it was named a National Treasure in 1970.
It now belongs to the Kansong Art Museum.
Shin was born in 1758 into a family of court painters; his father and his grandfather both worked for the royal court.
He is remembered above all for delicate scenes of romance and of city pleasures.
First, look at the moon at the upper left.
Curiously, this oddly shaped moon bulges upward.
One astronomer argued that a moon can only look like this while the Earth's shadow is passing across it.
He read it as a partial lunar eclipse and even proposed a date: the night of 21 August 1793, when a court diary records an eclipse.
It may be the only love scene in Korean art to become a subject of astronomy.
Below the moon, dark foliage and the eaves of a tiled house deepen the night.
The house on the left and the wall slanting off to the right create a private corner, a small stage for just these two people.
Above them the artist wrote a line of verse: the moon is dim, the night is deep, and only these two know their hearts.
The hour it names falls around midnight, and at the end he signed his pen name, Hyewon.
Now to their faces.
She holds the edge of her cloak closed at her chin and tips her head slightly down.
The scholar, in his tall black hat, turns his eyes quietly toward her.
In his hand hangs the lantern, a small reddish glow against his white robe.
It lights the path through the dark, but it cannot reveal what either of them is thinking.
Now look down at their feet.
His feet already point onward; she hangs back half a step, undecided.
Their feet, pointing in different directions, tell the story better than any words.
Shin Yun-bok never explains; he lets empty space and glances carry the story.
Fine lines and pale colour keep everything understated, and that very restraint is what builds the quiet tension of the scene.
Now take a step back.
Are they about to set off together, or about to part here at the corner?
As the verse says, the answer belongs only to the two of them.
